newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans vow to help Washington.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans vow to help Washington.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican congressional leaders agreed on Tuesday to work together on the problems in the nation's capital, including a high crime rate, crumbling schools and weak finances.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told reporters after a meeting with Clinton that they agreed to form a joint administration-congressional task force on ways to improve near-bankrupt District of Columbia.
"This is our nation's capital. There is a crisis here," said Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
"We have a unique federal responsibility for our national capital," added Gingrich, a Georgia Republican.

The District of Columbia, which is a federal enclave rather than a state, is run by a mayor and a city council but gets much of its funds from Congress and its laws are subject to congressional review.

Washington officials have asked the White House and Congress for help but said they do not want the federal government to run the city as it did for more than a century until home rule was granted two decades ago.

"We can really focus on helping children in the district learn to read and really develop a measurable, observable effort right here in our national capital. And there was broad agreement on helping the district and helping the children of the district," Gingrich said.

"The president made some suggestions with regards to the District of Columbia -- how we can get the Congress involved, the administration involved with people in the District of Columbia. We cannot ignore this problem. We must find a way to work with the District of Columbia," Lott said.

"We ought to try some things here, maybe even experiment, and if it works here, then we could take it to the rest of the country -- to Newt's state, my state, and Michigan and every place else," Lott added.

Clinton and the others at the meeting said they made progress toward reaching bipartisan agreements. "It is an indication we want to work together," Clinton said afterwards, while Lott said, "You are going to see actions begin to happen as a result of this meeting today."

The district's problems were one of several topics discussed by Clinton and Republican and Democratic congressional leaders along with the federal budget, national education goals, tax cut proposals, welfare changes and juvenile crime.
